title: The Task Finished. Did It Help? | SideFX Episode 2
visualGrammar: principle decision plates; instructional composition; no authored circuit is required

scenes.title: The task finished. Did it help?
scenes.label: THE QUESTION
headline: The task finished.
Did it help?
scenes.body: A completed action. A result people can use. Are they the same?
scenes.narration: The task is finished. The confirmation arrived. But did it help? Before we talk about artificial intelligence, consider an ordinary decision: arranging an outing for a group of people.

scenes.title: A confirmed reservation
scenes.label: A FICTIONAL WEEKEND OUTING
headline: The room is booked.
cards: Two members cannot attend: the time conflicts with their last bus home.
scenes.narration: A volunteer reserves a room for a weekend group outing. The booking is confirmed. But the time conflicts with the last bus home for two members. They say they cannot attend at that time.

scenes.title: Who can decide?
scenes.label: THE DECISION
headline: “The reservation succeeded,
so the outing is arranged.”
scenes.body: The volunteer can ask about options. Only the coordinator can commit to a booking change.
scenes.narration: The volunteer can ask about another slot. Only the group coordinator can commit to changing the booking. The coordinator says: The reservation succeeded, so the outing is arranged.

scenes.title: Pause and make your call
scenes.label: YOUR FIRST JUDGMENT
headline: What should happen next?
Why?
scenes.body: Pause the video. Write your decision before hearing the discussion.
scenes.narration: What should happen next, and why? Pause the video and write your decision before hearing the discussion. You can leave the final choice open if you explain what you still need to know.

scenes.title: Choose what helps explain it
scenes.label: BEFORE THE PLATE
headline: Would a table help?
What would it leave out?
scenes.body: A written account is also a valid choice.
scenes.narration: Would a small table help you explain this situation? Or would a written account preserve something the table loses? Either can work. Keep the affected people and the unresolved facts in view.

scenes.title: Separate action, result, and uncertainty
scenes.label: A DECISION PLATE
headline: Is the outing arranged for
the people who need it?
cards: An outing the intended participants can actually attend.
Two report a travel conflict. Other times and costs are unknown.
scenes.narration: Here is one way to separate the facts. What happened: a room reservation was confirmed. What people need: an outing the intended participants can actually attend. What remains open: two members report a travel conflict. Other times and costs are unknown.

scenes.title: What the confirmation proves
scenes.label: THE LIMIT OF THE EVIDENCE
headline: A booking record proves
a reservation.
scenes.body: It does not prove that everyone can attend.
scenes.narration: The booking record supports a narrow claim: there is a reservation. It does not establish that everyone can attend. A defensible next step is to ask about alternatives and hear the affected members before promising that the outing is fully arranged.

scenes.title: An objection that matters
scenes.label: CHALLENGE YOUR FIRST ANSWER
headline: Moving it could exclude
someone else.
scenes.body: Some people have already planned around the original time.
scenes.narration: Now another organizer objects. People have already planned around this time. Moving the outing could inconvenience them, or exclude someone else. That objection matters. Asking about alternatives does not yet justify changing the booking.

scenes.title: Compare the consequences
scenes.label: OPTIONS TO DISCUSS
headline: Who bears the cost
of each option?
cards:
A different time.
Travel support, if feasible.

Postponement.
Keeping the booking while explicitly acknowledging the exclusion.
scenes.narration: Compare a different time, travel support if it is feasible, postponement, and keeping the booking with the exclusion explicitly acknowledged. Hear from the people who bear each cost. The coordinator has a decision role. That role does not make every choice fair.

scenes.title: What would change your judgment?
scenes.label: REVISE WITH A REASON
headline: What would change
your judgment?
scenes.body: Name a specific fact that could change your next step.
scenes.narration: What would change your judgment? Name a specific fact that could change your next step. Pause and write it down.

scenes.title: New facts can change the next step
scenes.label: CONDITIONAL EXAMPLES
headline: New facts can change
the next step.
scenes.body: An acceptable travel option? A different time that excludes more people? These are possibilities, not facts in the story.
scenes.narration: Perhaps the two members identify an acceptable travel option. Perhaps a different time would exclude more people. Neither is established in this story. Either could change the next step. Neither would make the original confirmation proof that the whole arrangement worked.

scenes.title: Completion is one fact
scenes.label: CONSEQUENCES · SIDEFX FOUNDATIONS
headline: Completion is one fact.
Consequences need judgment.
scenes.body: Which result do you mean? Who still cannot get what they need?
scenes.narration: A conversation and a list of alternatives may be enough. Changing a booking does not necessarily recover preparation time or missed participation. This is the consequences lens we are starting with in SideFX: when someone says a task is complete, ask which result they mean, and who still cannot get what they need.

scenes.title: Carry the question with you
scenes.label: CONTINUE THE PRACTICE
headline: Choose one completed task.
Whose result is still open?
scenes.body:
Describe the missing result and the evidence you would need.
Next: What do we actually know?
scenes.narration: Think of one completed task in your own work. Whose result might still be unresolved? Describe the missing result and the evidence you would need. Next, we will ask: What do we actually know?
